```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

Everything matchdb downloads or writes goes in one folder. This article covers:

* what goes in that folder;
* the three ways to get data, and what each costs;
* the log of everything fetched, compiled and published;
* updating to a new release, and finding out why match results moved.

## One folder

The folder is `md_data_root()`. It is the `MATCHDB_DATA` environment variable
if you set one, and `~/Documents/matchdb` otherwise. Set it in `.Renviron` to
keep the data on a larger drive:

```
MATCHDB_DATA=D:/matchdb
```

Its layout is fixed:

```
matchdb/
  tranches/<build>/        the database as parquet, split by layer and class
  tranches/latest.json     the build md_tranche_db() opens by default
  publish/<label>/<hash>/  compiled references (bundles)
  db/MATCHDB.duckdb        the whole database, if you download it
  logs/runs-index.csv      one row per action, never rewritten
  logs/<kind>-<run>.csv    the detail of one action
  logs/state.json          what is here now
```

## Three ways to get data

| you want | call | download |
|---|---|---:|
| one of the four published tiers | `md_reference("active-observed", fetch = "missing")` | 280–470 MB |
| your own spec | `md_fetch_tranches(spec)` | about 1 GB for an active-layer spec |
| everything, to browse | `md_fetch_db()` | 11.8 GB |

The output below is from the build of 2026-11-01, fetched into an empty folder
with npnormalize 0.1.3 installed.

For your own spec, see what it will cost first. `md_tranches()` reads the
published build's manifest and marks the files the spec needs:

```{r}
s <- md_spec(layers = "bmf_active", names = c("legal", "dba"), addresses = "mailing")
md_tranches(s)
#> <md_tranches 2026-11-01-67c0bd2f> built 2026-11-01 from matchdb@a79e519, normalizer v1-592912060053c4c3
#>   108 files, 4.53 GB; here: 0 files, 0.00 GB
#>   this spec needs 17 files, 1.01 GB; still to download: 17 files, 1.01 GB
#>              table         layer files     rows    mb here
#>            address    bmf_active     3 13568639 856.1    0
#>   ...
```

Then fetch those files, open them, and compile:

```{r}
md_fetch_tranches(s)
#> tranches 2026-11-01-67c0bd2f: 17 files here (0 already were, 0 copied from an older build), 1.01 GB downloaded
con <- md_tranche_db()
r <- md_compile(s, con)          # 2,742,710 rows, about a minute
md_db_close(con)
```

`md_tranche_manifest()` returns the build's whole manifest:

* the build id;
* when it was built, and from which matchdb commit;
* the normalizer it was built with, and the npnormalize and npmatch versions;
* every file's rows, bytes and md5.

A copy of the manifest is kept in the build's folder. It records what you
downloaded, even after the files themselves are deleted.

### Why parquet files, and not a local database

The downloaded parquet files are the local copy. `md_tranche_db()` opens them
in an in-memory DuckDB, as one view per table, and copies nothing. matchdb
does not build a second database from them, for three reasons:

* Each file can be checked against its md5, alone. A database built from them
  could only be checked as a whole.
* A second spec adds only the files it is missing, and a new release reuses
  every file that did not change. A database would have to be rebuilt.
* Compiling from the files takes about a minute, so a database would save
  little time and double the disk used.

What is worth saving is the compiled reference. `md_publish()` writes it as a
bundle under `publish/`, and `md_reference()` reads it back in seconds.

## The log

Every fetch, compile and publish adds one row to `logs/runs-index.csv`. Rows
are never changed or removed. Each row records:

* what was done, and when;
* the tranche build and spec;
* how many files were downloaded, copied from an older build, reused or
  failed, and the bytes moved;
* the installed matchdb, npnormalize, npmatch and normalizer signature.

```{r}
md_log()[, c("run_id", "kind", "build", "spec_hash", "files", "downloaded", "bytes")]
#>                   run_id           kind               build        spec_hash files downloaded      bytes
#> 1 20261101T130816-243823 fetch_tranches 2026-11-01-67c0bd2f 2402137493f88c8e    17         17 1005899238
#> 2 20261101T130925-243875        compile 2026-11-01-67c0bd2f 2402137493f88c8e    NA         NA         NA
```

`md_log_run()` returns one action's detail. For a fetch, that is every file
with its source URL, status, rows, bytes and md5, plus the manifest it came
from. For a compile, it is the spec, the stamp and the shape of the result:

```{r}
md_log_run("20261101T130816-243823")
```

`md_status()` describes what is here now. It covers the installed versions,
the current build and how much of it is downloaded, the database, the
bundles, and the last compile. The same record is written to
`logs/state.json` after every action:

```{r}
md_status()
#> <md_status> D:/matchdb
#>   installed  matchdb 0.1.1.9000, npnormalize 0.1.3, npmatch 0.1.1.9000 @7ea7447, normalizer v1-592912060053c4c3
#>   tranches   2026-11-01-67c0bd2f (built 2026-11-01, normalizer v1-592912060053c4c3): 17 of 108 files here, 1.01 GB
#>   database   none
#>   last compile 2026-11-01T13:09:25: spec 2402137493f88c8e, 2,742,710 rows, from tranches 2026-11-01-67c0bd2f
#>   last action  2026-11-01T13:09:25 compile (run 20261101T130925-243875)
```

## Updating to a new release

A new release is a new build, in a new folder. Nothing in the old one is
overwritten. To see what changed before downloading anything, compare the
build you have with the newest. Here is the update of 2026-11-01, from the
2026-10-27 build:

```{r}
md_tranche_diff("2026-10-27-82c6f0cb")      # your build against the newest
#> <md_tranche_diff> 2026-10-27-82c6f0cb -> 2026-11-01-67c0bd2f
#>   normalize_signature  v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e -> v1-592912060053c4c3
#>   npnormalize_version  ? -> 0.1.3
#>   npmatch_version      0.1.0.9000 -> 0.1.1.9000
#>   matchdb_commit       592b078 -> a79e519
#>   db_fingerprint       a0774546e057f983  (same)
#>   The normalizer changed: every derived column may differ, and match results with it.
#>   files: same 47, changed 61, added 0, removed 0
#>   to download for the whole build: 2.36 GB of 4.53 GB
#>              table         layer  status files rows_change
#>    address_compact       (whole) changed     1       -1629
#>    address_derived    bmf_active changed     3           0
#>   ...
#>         place_unit       (whole) changed     1       -1399
#>   ...
```

The diff lists:

* every file as same, changed, added or removed, with its change in rows;
* whether the normalizer, the npnormalize or npmatch version, or the matchdb
  commit changed;
* how much a full update would download.

The `?` is the older build's npnormalize version: builds made before matchdb
took the normalizer from npnormalize did not record it.

This update is a new normalizer over the same data (the `db_fingerprint` did
not change). So every `*_derived` file changed, along with everything built
from the keys: the compact tables, the place tables and the clusters. The raw
`name`, `address` and `entity` files did not.

Then fetch as before. Files whose md5 matches one in your older build are
copied from it rather than downloaded. For the spec above, 7 of its 17 files
are the same in both builds (0.66 GB). An update from the 2026-10-27 build
copies those and downloads the other 10 (0.35 GB).

Copying is how you see a release's effect on disk, not only on the matches.
A data update with the same normalizer leaves more files the same.

Rows are not added to old files. Every build recomputes, over the whole
database:

* the normalized columns;
* the statistics cells;
* the clusters and the compact tables.

So a release can change a file whose own rows did not change. Copying
unchanged files saves the downloads that can be saved, and the whole build
always stays consistent.

When the new build works, `md_tranches_prune()` deletes the old build's
parquet files and keeps its manifest:

```{r}
md_tranches_prune(keep = 1)
```

## When match results change

A match can move for two reasons:

* the data changed: a new build;
* the matching changed: a new npnormalize or npmatch, above all a new
  normalizer.

The log records both. Before each action it compares the installed npnormalize,
npmatch and normalizer with what the last action used. If they differ, it adds a
`version_change` row first. Fetching a different build or database adds one
too:

```{r}
md_log("version_change")[, c("recorded_at", "note")]
#> (an illustration: the two rows an update from 2026-10-27 to 2026-11-01 writes)
#>   recorded_at  note
#>   ...          normalize_signature v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e -> v1-592912060053c4c3; npnormalize_version 0.1.1 -> 0.1.3
#>   ...          tranches 2026-10-27-82c6f0cb -> 2026-11-01-67c0bd2f: files same 47 changed 61 added 0 removed 0;
#>                  name+address+entity rows +0; normalizer v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e -> v1-592912060053c4c3
```

Read these rows next to the compiles around them. They show which build and
which normalizer produced each set of results.

A build made by another normalizer is refused rather than used:
`md_tranche_db()` and `md_reference()` stop with an error naming both
signatures. Install the matching npnormalize, or fetch a build made with yours:

```{r}
md_reference("active-observed")
#> Error: bundle active-observed/9cc7b76e3e144a87 was built by normalizer
#>   v1-592912060053c4c3; the installed one is v1-1179714ce1e9d31f. ...
```

That is what npnormalize 0.1.4 gives against the data published on 2026-11-01.
To get the right normalizer, install npnormalize at the commit the data was
built with (`6d9c669` for 0.1.3), or wait for a build made with the newer one.
`vignette("updates")` explains when and why a rebuild happens.

To turn logging off, set `options(matchdb.log = FALSE)`.
